Problem Statement¶

Context¶

AllLife Bank is a US bank that has a growing customer base. The majority of these customers are liability customers (depositors) with varying sizes of deposits. The number of customers who are also borrowers (asset customers) is quite small, and the bank is interested in expanding this base rapidly to bring in more loan business and in the process, earn more through the interest on loans. In particular, the management wants to explore ways of converting its liability customers to personal loan customers (while retaining them as depositors).

A campaign that the bank ran last year for liability customers showed a healthy conversion rate of over 9% success. This has encouraged the retail marketing department to devise campaigns with better target marketing to increase the success ratio.

You as a Data scientist at AllLife bank have to build a model that will help the marketing department to identify the potential customers who have a higher probability of purchasing the loan.

Objective¶

To predict whether a liability customer will buy personal loans, to understand which customer attributes are most significant in driving purchases, and identify which segment of customers to target more.

Data Dictionary¶

  • ID: Customer ID
  • Age: Customer’s age in completed years
  • Experience: #years of professional experience
  • Income: Annual income of the customer (in thousand dollars)
  • ZIP Code: Home Address ZIP code.
  • Family: the Family size of the customer
  • CCAvg: Average spending on credit cards per month (in thousand dollars)
  • Education: Education Level. 1: Undergrad; 2: Graduate;3: Advanced/Professional
  • Mortgage: Value of house mortgage if any. (in thousand dollars)
  • Personal_Loan: Did this customer accept the personal loan offered in the last campaign? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • Securities_Account: Does the customer have securities account with the bank? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • CD_Account: Does the customer have a certificate of deposit (CD) account with the bank? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • Online: Do customers use internet banking facilities? (0: No, 1: Yes)
  • CreditCard: Does the customer use a credit card issued by any other Bank (excluding All life Bank)? (0: No, 1: Yes)

Examples
--------

    The simplest way to use nbconvert is

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to html

            Options include ['asciidoc', 'custom', 'html', 'latex', 'markdown', 'notebook', 'pdf', 'python', 'qtpdf', 'qtpng', 'rst', 'script', 'slides', 'webpdf'].

            > jupyter nbconvert --to latex mynotebook.ipynb

            Both HTML and LaTeX support multiple output templates. LaTeX includes
            'base', 'article' and 'report'.  HTML includes 'basic', 'lab' and
            'classic'. You can specify the flavor of the format used.

            > jupyter nbconvert --to html --template lab mynotebook.ipynb

            You can also pipe the output to stdout, rather than a file

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --stdout

            PDF is generated via latex

            > jupyter nbconvert mynotebook.ipynb --to pdf

            You can get (and serve) a Reveal.js-powered slideshow

            > jupyter nbconvert myslides.ipynb --to slides --post serve

            Multiple notebooks can be given at the command line in a couple of
            different ways:

            > jupyter nbconvert notebook*.ipynb
            > jupyter nbconvert notebook1.ipynb notebook2.ipynb

            or you can specify the notebooks list in a config file, containing::

                c.NbConvertApp.notebooks = ["my_notebook.ipynb"]

            > jupyter nbconvert --config mycfg.py

To see all available configurables, use `--help-all`.

Exploratory Data Analysis.¶

  • EDA is an important part of any project involving data.
  • It is important to investigate and understand the data better before building a model with it.
  • A few questions have been mentioned below which will help you approach the analysis in the right manner and generate insights from the data.
  • A thorough analysis of the data, in addition to the questions mentioned below, should be done.

Questions:

  1. What is the distribution of mortgage attribute? Are there any noticeable patterns or outliers in the distribution?

Distribution: The mortgage attribute shows a right-skewed distribution, with a significant portion of customers having no mortgage (value = 0). A smaller group has high mortgage values, which creates the positive skew.

Patterns: The majority of customers do not hold a mortgage, suggesting they might be renters or homeowners without outstanding loans.

Outliers: A few customers have significantly high mortgage values, which stand out in the dataset. These outliers might need attention during model training as they could influence results disproportionately.

  1. How many customers have credit cards?

Credit Card Users: Based on the CreditCard attribute, around 29.2% of the customers use credit cards issued by banks other than AllLife Bank. This means that approximately 1,460 customers out of the total 5,000 have credit cards.

  1. What are the attributes that have a strong correlation with the target attribute (personal loan)?

Income: Higher income levels are strongly associated with customers accepting personal loans.

CCAvg (Credit Card Average Usage): Customers with higher credit card spending are more likely to accept personal loans.

Education: Customers with advanced or professional education levels show a higher tendency to take loans.

CD Account: Having a Certificate of Deposit account increases the likelihood of loan acceptance.

These correlations suggest that financially stable and educated customers are more inclined toward personal loans.

  1. How does a customer's interest in purchasing a loan vary with their age? Age Trends:

Younger customers, particularly those in their 20s and 30s, are more likely to take personal loans. This could be due to their financial needs for education, starting a career, or other life investments.

Interest in loans gradually decreases with age. Customers in their 50s and 60s show a reduced likelihood of taking loans, possibly due to being more financially secure or debt-averse.

The trend suggests a negative correlation between age and loan acceptance.

  1. How does a customer's interest in purchasing a loan vary with their education? Educational Trends:

Customers with higher education levels (Graduate and Advanced/Professional degrees) are significantly more likely to accept loans. This might be because they are more aware of the benefits of borrowing for investment or have higher earning potential.

Customers with undergraduate education show lower rates of loan acceptance compared to the other groups.

Education is an essential factor for segmenting and targeting customers.

def histogram_boxplot_alt(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Alternative Boxplot and Histogram combined.

    data: dataframe
    feature: column in the dataframe
    figsize: size of figure (default (12, 7))
    kde: whether to include a density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    # Create the figure and define layout with GridSpec
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=figsize)
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 1, height_ratios=[1, 3], hspace=0.1)

    # Add boxplot on the first row
    ax_box = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, 0])
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box, showmeans=True, color="lightblue")
    ax_box.set(xlabel="")

    # Add histogram on the second row
    ax_hist = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0])
    sns.histplot(data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist, bins=bins, color="skyblue")

    # Add mean and median lines
    ax_hist.axvline(data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--", label="Mean")
    ax_hist.axvline(data[feature].median(), color="orange", linestyle="-", label="Median")
    ax_hist.legend()

    # Finalize layout
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def labeled_barplot_alt(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with labels on top.

    data: dataframe
    feature: column in the dataframe
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of counts (default False)
    n: display the top n categories (default None: show all categories)
    """
    # Determine the number of unique categories and total entries
    total = data[feature].size
    unique_count = data[feature].nunique()

    # Set up figure size based on the number of categories
    fig_size = unique_count + 1 if n is None else n + 1
    plt.figure(figsize=(fig_size, 5))

    # Configure x-axis labels
    plt.xticks(rotation=45, fontsize=12)

    # Create the barplot
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="coolwarm",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n],
    )

    # Add annotations to the bars
    for bar in ax.patches:
        height = bar.get_height()
        if perc:
            label = f"{(100 * height / total):.1f}%"  # Calculate percentage
        else:
            label = f"{height}"  # Use count

        x = bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2
        y = height

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="bottom",
            fontsize=10,
            color="black",
            xytext=(0, 4),  # Offset text slightly above the bar
            textcoords="offset points",
        )

    # Display the barplot
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def plot_distribution_against_target(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Function to visualize the relationship between a predictor and target variable
    through distribution plots and boxplots.
    """
    # Create a figure with a 2x2 grid layout
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 10))

    # Get the unique values of the target variable
    unique_targets = data[target].unique()

    # Plot the distribution for the first unique target value
    axs[0, 0].set_title(f"Distribution of {predictor} for {target}={unique_targets[0]}")
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == unique_targets[0]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 0],
        color="teal",
        stat="density",
    )

    # Plot the distribution for the second unique target value
    axs[0, 1].set_title(f"Distribution of {predictor} for {target}={unique_targets[1]}")
    sns.histplot(
        data=data[data[target] == unique_targets[1]],
        x=predictor,
        kde=True,
        ax=axs[0, 1],
        color="orange",
        stat="density",
    )

    # Plot the boxplot of predictor against the target variable
    axs[1, 0].set_title("Boxplot of Predictor w.r.t Target")
    sns.boxplot(data=data, x=target, y=predictor, ax=axs[1, 0], palette="gist_rainbow")

    # Plot the boxplot without outliers
    axs[1, 1].set_title("Boxplot of Predictor w.r.t Target (Outliers Removed)")
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data,
        x=target,
        y=predictor,
        ax=axs[1, 1],
        showfliers=False,
        palette="gist_rainbow",
    )

    # Adjust layout for better spacing
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf
In [118]:
def confusion_matrix_sklearn(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

In [61]:
# Choose the type of classifier.
estimator = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1)

# Grid of parameters to choose from
parameters = {
    "max_depth": np.arange(6, 15),
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2, 5, 7, 10],
    "max_leaf_nodes": [2, 3, 5, 10],
}

# Type of scoring used to compare parameter combinations
acc_scorer = make_scorer(recall_score)

# Run the grid search
grid_obj = GridSearchCV(estimator, parameters, scoring=acc_scorer, cv=5)
grid_obj = grid_obj.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Set the clf to the best combination of parameters

# Plot bar chart for training recall
ax.bar(
    x_positions - bar_width / 2,  # Offset for training bars
    recall_train,
    bar_width,
    label="Train",
    color="skyblue",
    alpha=0.8,
)

# Plot bar chart for testing recall
ax.bar(
    x_positions + bar_width / 2,  # Offset for testing bars
    recall_test,
    bar_width,
    label="Test",
    color="orange",
    alpha=0.8,
)

# Add labels, title, and legend
ax.set_xticks(x_positions)
ax.set_xticklabels([f"{alpha:.2f}" for alpha in ccp_alphas], rotation=45)
ax.set_xlabel("Alpha", fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("Recall", fontsize=12)
ax.set_title("Recall vs Alpha for Training and Testing Sets (Bar Chart)", fontsize=14)
ax.legend(loc="best")

# Display the plot
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

  • What recommedations would you suggest to the bank?

Recommendations to the bank¶

  1. Target Specific Demographics: Focus marketing efforts on customers with higher income levels, as they show an increased likelihood of accepting personal loans. Younger customers (in their 20s to 30s) appear more inclined to take personal loans. Tailor campaigns to address their needs like student loans, travel expenses, or business opportunities.

  2. Credit Card Users: Customers with credit cards seem to have a strong correlation with loan acceptance. Create special loan offers for these customers to encourage borrowing.

  3. Educational Insights: Customers with advanced education levels (professional or graduate degrees) demonstrate a higher probability of taking loans. Highlight loan benefits for career advancements, professional certifications, or home investments in campaigns targeted at these groups.

  4. Upsell to Existing Depositors: Customers with a Certificate of Deposit (CD) account or securities account already have a strong relationship with the bank. Offer exclusive loan rates or benefits to these loyal customers to deepen the relationship.

  5. Leverage Online Banking: Customers using online banking are more engaged and tech-savvy. Utilize digital channels for personalized marketing campaigns and easy loan application processes.

  6. Encourage High Credit Card Spending: Customers with higher average credit card usage (CCAvg) are potential candidates for personal loans. Create targeted campaigns offering cashbacks or lower interest loans for this segment.

  7. Refine Loan Offers: Analyze family size trends, as customers from families with medium sizes (e.g., 2-3 members) might need loans for housing or education. Tailor promotions to address these needs.

  8. Geographical Segmentation: Use the ZIP code information to design region-specific campaigns where loan uptake is higher. This targeted approach can optimize resource allocation.
